title: Infra GPU fleet: capacity, networking, Terraform modules & CI/CD playbook
author: Priya Shah
content:
Overview

This document is the canonical infra team playbook for operating the GPU fleet and related infrastructure: capacity planning, cloud accounts & networking, Terraform/IaC module patterns, CI/CD build pipelines, and key runbooks. It is intended for infra engineers, SREs, and platform owners responsible for Redwood Inference dedicated and private offerings.

Goals
- Provide repeatable guidance for adding capacity and networking for GPU clusters.
- Standardize Terraform modules and CI/CD patterns to reduce drift and increase safety.
- Document operational runbooks for common incidents and day-2 ops.

Scope
Includes: GPU fleet sizing (NVIDIA A100/H100/BF16/8-bit variants), cloud account topology and VPCs, firewall and routing patterns, Terraform modules and examples, CI/CD pipelines for IaC and runtime images, and runbooks for capacity events, kernel upgrades, and service degradation. Excludes: model onboarding (see applied-ml-and-evals), customer-specific private deployment runbooks (stored in eng-private-deployments).

Ownership and Roles
- Fleet Owner: infra-gpu (primary contact: @Marcus Lee)
- Networking: infra-networking (primary contact: @Aisha Patel)
- IaC / CI: infra-platform (primary contact: @Priya Shah)
- Oncall SRE: eng-sre rotation (see rota in team wiki)

High-level workflow (summary)
1) Capacity request is submitted via the capacity playbook form (link) and triaged.
2) Infra evaluates quotas, region requirements, and networking impacts.
3) Terraform module changes are proposed in a feature branch; pipeline runs plan + policy checks.
4) Post-approval, apply is executed via CI with staged rollout and smoke-tests.
5) Monitoring & cost dashboards validated for 48h; rollback if regressions.

Capacity Planning
- Target utilization: steady-state 55% GPU memory utilization per-instance and 65% average scheduler utilization to allow headroom for burst workloads.
- Scale trigger thresholds:
  - Scale-up: cluster average GPU memory utilization > 70% for 30m and queue latency > 200ms P95.
  - Scale-down: cluster average GPU memory utilization < 40% for 60m and queue latency < 80ms P95.
- Safety buffer: maintain at least 10% spare capacity on Dedicated clusters to allow fast tail-latency requests and node replacement during upgrades.

GPU Types & Sizing (recommendations)
- A100 80GB: default for large context long-running inference. Use for models > 13B with KV caching.
- H100 80GB: preferred for throughput-sensitive high-concurrency workloads; use when INT8/Half kernels required.
- A10/A30: cost-efficient option for mid-size models and embeddings.
- Example sizing guidelines (rough):
  - 7B dense model: 1 x A10 per 12 concurrent workers
  - 13B quantized: 1 x A100 per 6 concurrent workers
  - 70B/llama-class: 1 x H100 per 1-2 workers depending on sequence length

Cloud Accounts & Networking
- Account layout: per-environment account model (prod, staging, sandbox) with separate billing tags and least-privilege sub-accounts for partner projects.
- VPC topology: hub-and-spoke design. Hub contains shared services (NAT, centralized logging, transit gateway). Spokes map to clusters and customer-private subnets.
- Subneting and security groups:
  - Management subnets (private) for nodes and kube control plane.
  - Public bastion in dedicated management subnet for restricted ssh access (jump host).
  - GPU clusters restricted via security groups: only ingress from internal services and monitoring CIDRs.
- Transit and peering: use cloud transit gateway / shared VPC for cross-account routing; avoid per-cluster peering to reduce configuration complexity.
- Firewall rules and egress controls: Egress NAT with destination allowlist for model download endpoints and container registries. Block direct internet access from runtime nodes except approved endpoints.

Terraform / IaC Modules (standards)
- Module design principles:
  - Small, single-responsibility modules (vpc, subnet, firewall, gpu-node-pool, iam-role, iam-policy, eks-cluster).
  - Inputs and outputs named explicitly; avoid implicit side-effects.
  - Use versioned module releases and lock module versions in root module via registry (module_version variable).
- Mandatory checks in PRs:
  1) terraform fmt and validate
  2) terraform plan in a sandbox account and plan output uploaded to PR
  3) policy-as-code (Sentinel/OPA) checks for IAM and network exposure
  4) cost-estimation check (estimated monthly spend)
- Example module usage (simplified):
```
module "gpu_node_pool" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@internal/modules.git//gpu-node-pool?ref=v1.3.0"
  cluster_id = module.eks.cluster_id
  instance_type = "nvidia-a100-80gb"
  desired_capacity = 6
  min_size = 2
  max_size = 12
  taints = [{ key = "dedicated", value = "gpu" , effect = "NO_SCHEDULE" }]
}
```

- Recommended Terraform settings in root module:
  - required_version = ">= 1.4.0"
  - backend: remote (our Terraform Cloud workspace per-account)
  - lock state via remote runs; apply only from CI role.

CI/CD and Build Pipelines
- Pipeline types:
  - IaC pipeline: format -> validate -> plan (in sandbox) -> policy checks -> manual approval -> apply (via service account).
  - Image build pipeline: build runtime images (from CODEBASE) -> scan (SCA + container CVE) -> sign image -> push to internal registry -> tag and publish.
  - Release pipeline: orchestrates cluster rollout, node replacement, and smoke tests.
- Best practices:
  - No direct human 'terraform apply' from laptop. All applies are executed by CI with recorded audit logs.
  - Use environment-specific workspaces and per-account service principals with fine-grained permissions.
  - Canary-scale: Deploy new node-pool with 5% of traffic; shift 25% after 30m if metrics OK, then 100% after 4h.
- Example CI job (GitHub Actions / self-hosted runner snippet):
```
jobs:
  terraform:
    runs-on: [self-hosted, linux, terraform]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Setup Terraform
        uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v1
      - name: terraform fmt
        run: terraform fmt -check
      - name: terraform init
        run: terraform init -backend-config="workspace=${{ matrix.workspace }}"
      - name: terraform plan
        run: terraform plan -out=plan.out
      - name: upload plan
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
        with:
          name: tf-plan
          path: plan.out
```

Runbooks (operational)
- GPU capacity alarm: high-utilization (P95 queue latency > 250ms)
  1) Pager fires to infra-oncall.
  2) Run `kubectl top nodes` and `kubectl get pods -A -o wide | grep Evicted`.
  3) Check autoscaler events: `kubectl describe hpa` / `kubectl describe clusterautoscaler`.
  4) If scaling blocked due to quotas, escalate to CloudOps to request quota increase; open cloud support ticket with reference: "redwood-gpu-urgent".
  5) Short-term mitigation: scale up node-pool via the emergency-scaling pipeline (button in console) which creates X new spot/dedicated nodes in target region.
  6) Post-incident: run capacity retrospective and update the capacity model.

- Node replacement for kernel driver/security update
  1) Create new node-pool with updated AMI/kernel and taint it to avoid scheduling: `kubectl cordon` existing nodes as you migrate.
  2) Drain nodes: `kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data` following staggered schedule (max 10% parallel).
  3) Validate workloads and GPU performance (latency and mem usage) for 1h per batch.
  4) Decommission old node-pool via IaC.

- Image vulnerability alert (critical CVE)
  1) Trigger: image-scan pipeline flags critical CVE in runtime image.
  2) Create hotfix branch, bump base image or patch package, run CI image build + scan.
  3) Canary push and deploy to canary cluster; monitor CPU/GPU and inference error rates.
  4) Roll out to prod via controlled canary and incremental shift.

Dashboards & Metrics (baseline set)
- Cluster-level:
  - GPU memory utilization (avg, P95)
  - GPU SM utilization (avg)
  - Job queue length and P95 latency
  - Node replacement rate and drain failures
- Cost & capacity:
  - Estimated monthly GPU spend by region and instance type
  - Preemptible/spot eviction rate
- Alerts:
  - GPU memory P95 > 80% for 10m (SEV-2)
  - Job queue P95 > 300ms for 10m (SEV-1)
  - Apply failure for IaC pipeline (blocker)

Change Management and Rollout Policy
- All infra changes affecting networking, IAM, or quota must have a roadmap ticket and at least two reviewers including a networking owner when relevant.
- Emergency changes require post-facto documentation and a retrospective within 72h.

Operational Playbook Checklist (pre-deploy)
1) Confirm account quotas and billing tags.
2) Validate Terraform plan output and estimated cost.
3) Ensure network peerings/transit routes exist for new region.
4) Smoke test: deploy sample job and validate end-to-end response and metrics.
5) Ensure monitoring, logs, and S3/gcs destinations for perf traces are configured.

Appendix A: Quick Terraform module example (full minimal)
```
# modules/gpu-node-pool/main.tf (minimal example)
resource "aws_autoscaling_group" "gpu_pool" {
  name = "gpu-pool-${var.cluster_name}"
  launch_configuration = aws_launch_configuration.gpu_lc.id
  min_size = var.min_size
  max_size = var.max_size
  desired_capacity = var.desired_capacity
  vpc_zone_identifier = var.subnet_ids
  tag {
    key = "k8s.io/cluster-autoscaler/enabled"
    value = "true"
    propagate_at_launch = true
  }
}
```

Appendix B: Useful CLI snippets
- Check node GPU memory: `nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.used,memory.total --format=csv`
- Inspect autoscaler events: `kubectl logs deployment/cluster-autoscaler -n kube-system --since=1h`
